bib.title: One Billion Word Benchmark for Measuring Progress in Statistical Language Modeling
bib.venue: preprint (arXiv v3; INTERSPEECH 2014 per ledger, venue not printed in text)

question: How can progress in statistical language modeling be measured on a freely reproducible, large (about one billion word) corpus, and how do standard LM families compare on it?
hypothesis: A one-billion-word corpus balances relevance in a world of abundant data against ease of evaluation, and combining techniques will beat the n-gram baseline substantially.
contributions: A reproducible one-billion-word benchmark built from freely available WMT11 data, with scripts and per-word log-probabilities for baseline n-gram models
Strong baselines with neural network LMs, including the largest RNN LM reported at the time
Comparison of several LM families and their linear interpolation on the same data

method.summary: Builds a training/held-out corpus from WMT11 monolingual English text (dedup, tokenise, vocabulary cutoff, shuffle, partition), then trains Katz/KN n-grams, Stupid Backoff, binary MaxEnt, hierarchical-softmax MaxEnt and RNN+MaxEnt LMs and reports test perplexity, training time and linear interpolation.
method.task: word-level statistical language modeling (next-word prediction), perplexity evaluation

datasets.name: WMT11 monolingual English training corpora (1B Word Benchmark)
datasets.size: about 2.9 billion words before dedup; 829250940 words after duplicate-sentence removal (counting <S>, <\S>)
datasets.split: sentences shuffled, 100 disjoint partitions; 1 partition (1%) held out; held-out shuffled and split into 50 partitions for dev/test; one partition (2% of held-out, 159658 words) is the test set; rest reserved
datasets.preprocessing: WMT11 normalisation/tokenisation scripts augmented to normalise UTF-8 punctuation variants; duplicate sentences removed; vocabulary of 793471 words (count >= 3, incl. <S>, <\S>); OOV mapped to <UNK>; test OoV rate 0.28%; sentence order randomised so no cross-sentence context

other.pruning: Stolcke entropy pruning for the 15M versions

models.name: Stupid Backoff 5-gram
models.architecture: n-gram, unnormalised, normalised over vocabulary for perplexity

models.name: Hierarchical Softmax MaxEnt 4-gram (HME)
models.architecture: MaxEnt with binary Huffman tree hierarchical softmax

models.name: Recurrent NN-256/512/1024 + MaxEnt 9-gram
models.architecture: RNN LM (256, 512 or 1024 neurons) run in parallel with MaxEnt over 9 previous words plus previous 15 words as order-independent features

training.objective: inferred: maximum likelihood / perplexity minimisation (hyper-parameters chosen to minimise perplexity)
training.hardware: RNN: single standard machine without GPUs (24 CPUs per Table 1); n-gram 100 CPUs; Binary MaxEnt 5000 CPUs (500 machines for negative generation, 5000 for tuning); HME 1 CPU
training.wall_clock: RNN-256 60h, RNN-512 120h, RNN-1024 240h; KN 3h; Katz 2h; SBO 0.4h; Binary MaxEnt 1h / 1.25h; HME 3h; binary MaxEnt negative generation 7.25 h on 500 machines, tuning 50 and 70 min on 5000 machines

other.rnn_speedups: parallelisation across CPU threads, SIMD, 90% fewer output parameters, MaxEnt in parallel; claimed 20-50x faster training; details deferred to a later paper

metrics.name: perplexity
metrics.definition: test-set perplexity on the 159658-word test partition, <S> not predicted; SBO normalised over the vocabulary

eval.protocol: single test partition; interpolation weights tuned to minimise perplexity on held-out data; no seeds or significance tests

availability.code: scripts to rebuild data on code.google.com project (1-billion-word-language-modeling-benchmark)
availability.data: rebuildable from WMT11 monolingual data; per-word log-probabilities for baseline n-gram models on ten held-out sets released

limits: Sentence order is randomised, so the benchmark cannot test long-context dependencies across sentences (Section 2).
Training times are not comparable across models since they depend on implementation (Section 5.1).
Hyper-parameters tuned only for perplexity, not model size or speed; some well-known techniques are missing; limited collaborative effort.
No application-level (ASR, SMT) evaluation; authors suggest adding lattices/N-best lists.
RNN speed-up details deferred to an upcoming paper; no seeds or variance reported.
Dated: word-level vocab with perplexity on a news corpus; later neural LMs (LSTM, transformers) far surpassed these numbers.
